# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

1. Congress should ...

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention, Northgate Progress Institute
Published Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, about one death every 11 minutes, and firearms were the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year (CDC, 2023).

- The country recorded 656 mass shootings in 2023, leaving 712 people dead and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023). Hmm, "give FBI tools and staff" — fine as imperative to Congress (fund NICS).

4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grant programs for states that enact and implement extreme-risk protection orders with due process, so families and law enforcement can act before a threat becomes a headline, and fund training for judges and officers who carry them out.

DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW: Not for release. NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the CDC's final mortality data show: about one death every 11 minutes. Guns stayed the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed dealer sells a gun. Among owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years, 22% got it with no background check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and help states enact extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the CDC's final mortality data show. That is about one death every 11 minutes: roughly 128 people a day, every day, all year. Almost none of those deaths will make the national news. They happen in stairwells and garages and parked cars, to someone's parent, partner, child or friend.

No other high-income country lives with a toll like this, and none of ours is fixed in stone. It is the product of policy, of gaps in American gun law wide enough to walk through. Two of the widest gaps are the subject of this brief: a background check system that covers only part of the gun market, and assault weapons that Congress once banned and let back on the shelves.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than this one: in 2023, for the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for America's children and teens, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer (CDC, 2023). Firearms killed 2,566 children and teens that year.

Each of those children had a classroom and a bedroom and a place at a lunch table. What they did not have was a country that treated gun deaths as a preventable problem. Parents send children to schools that run active-shooter drills. Grief counselors have a permanent seat in American education. That is what normal looks like when the leading killer of children is a firearm.

Other wealthy nations have cars, mental illness, despairing teenagers and violent entertainment. What they do not have is our gun policy. The difference is the gun, and the laws that decide who gets one.

## 3. The background-check gap

When the background check system is used, it works. The National Instant Criminal Background Check System has processed more than 500 million checks since 1998 and logged more than 2 million denials of sales to people legally barred from owning firearms (FBI).

The gap is where the system stops. Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed firearms dealer makes the sale. Private sellers, including many at gun shows and those arranging sales online, face no such requirement in most of the country. The result is a two-tier market: one in which a prohibited purchaser is screened out, and one in which the same purchaser can buy the same gun, no questions asked.

How big is the unchecked tier? In the best national estimate available, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017). Roughly one acquisition in five. A felony record, a domestic violence conviction, a court's finding of dangerousness: none of it discovered, because nobody looked.

Americans broadly agree this should change. A 2022 national poll found 92% support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A policy with that kind of mandate is not waiting on public opinion. It is waiting on Congress.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 was a brutal year even by recent standards: 656 mass shootings, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023).

The massacres that define this era share a signature. At Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, 17 people were killed. At Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, 21 died, 19 of them children. In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, 18 were killed at a bowling alley and a bar. Each attack was carried out with a semiautomatic rifle and detachable high-capacity magazines, the configuration the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Congress enacted that ban in September 1994 as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, barring the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It let the law expire on Sept. 13, 2004, and the market rebuilt itself around the banned design. Federal evaluations found criminal use of the banned weapons declined while the ban was in force (National Institute of Justice).

Gun lobby counters that rifles of all types are used in a small share of gun murders, 297 of 10,265 gun murders in 2018, the FBI reports. But that is the wrong ledger for weapons designed for volume rather than concealment. When an active shooter carries a semiautomatic rifle, the attack kills nearly twice as many people: an average of 4.25 deaths when such a rifle is present, against 2.49 when it is not (de Jager et al., JAMA, September 2018). And the decade the ban was in force stands apart: mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the ban period than before or after it (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019).

## Recommendations

Congress should treat the leading killer of American children the way it treats every other leading cause of death: with urgency, funding and law. Four actions follow.

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check for every firearm sale and transfer, including private, gun show and online sales, with no exceptions, and appropriate the funds the FBI needs to process them.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 prohibition on assault weapons and on ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, and write the definition so copycat designs engineered around the old feature list are covered.
3. Fund gun violence prevention research. Establish a dedicated appropriations line for firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, building on the $25 million a year first appropriated in fiscal 2020 after a two-decade freeze, and scaled to the toll.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grants for states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws, with due process protections, and fund training for the courts and law enforcement agencies that must use them.

None of this is untested. Background checks already screen millions of sales a year and are backed by 92% of the country (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A federal assault weapons ban is not a thought experiment; it is a decade of American history, with data on both sides of it. The gaps are narrow, well documented and closable. The price of leaving them open was 46,728 lives in 2023.

DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW: Not for release. NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the CDC's final mortality data show: about one death every 11 minutes. Guns stayed the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed dealer sells a gun. Among owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years, 22% got it with no background check at all (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017).
- The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and help states enact extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, the CDC's final mortality data show. That is about one death every 11 minutes: roughly 128 people a day, every day, all year. Almost none of those deaths will make the national news. They happen in stairwells and garages and parked cars, to someone's parent, partner, child or friend.

No other high-income country lives with a toll like this, and none of ours is fixed in stone. It is the product of policy, of gaps in American gun law wide enough to walk through. Two of the widest gaps are the subject of this brief: a background check system that covers only part of the gun market, and assault weapons that Congress once banned and let back on the shelves.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than this one: in 2023, for the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for America's children and teens, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer (CDC, 2023). Firearms killed 2,566 children and teens that year.

Each of those children had a classroom and a bedroom and a place at a lunch table. What they did not have was a country that treated gun deaths as a preventable problem. Parents send children to schools that run active-shooter drills. Grief counselors have a permanent seat in American education. That is what normal looks like when the leading killer of children is a firearm.

Other wealthy nations have cars, mental illness, despairing teenagers and violent entertainment. What they do not have is our gun policy. The difference is the gun, and the laws that decide who gets one.

## 3. The background-check gap

When the background check system is used, it works. The National Instant Criminal Background Check System has processed more than 500 million checks since 1998 and logged more than 2 million denials of sales to people legally barred from owning firearms (FBI).

The gap is where the system stops. Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed firearms dealer makes the sale. Private sellers, including many at gun shows and those arranging sales online, face no such requirement in most of the country. The result is a two-tier market: one in which a prohibited purchaser is screened out, and one in which the same purchaser can buy the same gun, no questions asked.

How big is the unchecked tier? In the best national estimate available, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017). Roughly one acquisition in five. A felony record, a domestic violence conviction, a court's finding of dangerousness: none of it discovered, because nobody looked.

Americans broadly agree this should change. A 2022 national poll found 92% support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A policy with that kind of mandate is not waiting on public opinion. It is waiting on Congress.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 was a brutal year even by recent standards: 656 mass shootings, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023).

The massacres that define this era share a signature. At Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, 17 people were killed. At Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, 21 died, 19 of them children. In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, 18 were killed at a bowling alley and a bar. Each attack was carried out with a semiautomatic rifle and detachable high-capacity magazines, the configuration the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Congress enacted that ban in September 1994 as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, barring the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It let the law expire on Sept. 13, 2004, and the market rebuilt itself around the banned design. Federal evaluations found criminal use of the banned weapons declined while the ban was in force (National Institute of Justice).

Gun lobby counters that rifles of all types are used in a small share of gun murders, 297 of 10,265 gun murders in 2018, the FBI reports. But that is the wrong ledger for weapons designed for volume rather than concealment. When an active shooter carries a semiautomatic rifle, the attack kills nearly twice as many people: an average of 4.25 deaths when such a rifle is present, against 2.49 when it is not (de Jager et al., JAMA, September 2018). And the decade the ban was in force stands apart: mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely during the ban period than before or after it (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019).

## Recommendations

Congress should treat the leading killer of American children the way it treats every other leading cause of death: with urgency, funding and law. Four actions follow.

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check for every firearm sale and transfer, including private, gun show and online sales, with no exceptions, and appropriate the funds the FBI needs to process them.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 prohibition on assault weapons and on ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, and write the definition so copycat designs engineered around the old feature list are covered.
3. Fund gun violence prevention research. Establish a dedicated appropriations line for firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, building on the $25 million a year first appropriated in fiscal 2020 after a two-decade freeze, and scaled to the toll.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grants for states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws, with due process protections, and fund training for the courts and law enforcement agencies that must use them.

None of this is untested. Background checks already screen millions of sales a year and are backed by 92% of the country (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A federal assault weapons ban is not a thought experiment; it is a decade of American history, with data on both sides of it. The gaps are narrow, well documented and closable. The price of leaving them open was 46,728 lives in 2023.

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show: about one death every 11 minutes. Guns stayed the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, for the fourth consecutive year.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed dealer sells a gun. Among gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years, 22% did so without any background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017).
- The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and help states enact extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show. That is about one death every 11 minutes: roughly 128 people a day, every day, all year. Almost none of those deaths will make the national news. They happen in stairwells and garages and parked cars, to someone's parent, partner, child or friend.

No other high-income country lives with a toll like this. Ours is not fixed in stone, either. It is the product of policy, of gaps in American gun law wide enough to walk through. Two of the widest gaps are the subject of this brief: a background check system that covers only part of the gun market, and assault weapons that Congress once banned and let back on the shelves.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than this one: in 2023, for the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for America's children and teens, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer (CDC, 2023). Firearms killed 2,566 children and teens that year.

Each of those children had a classroom and a bedroom and a place at a lunch table. What they did not have was a country that treated gun deaths as a preventable problem. Parents send children to schools that run active-shooter drills. Grief counselors have become a fixture of American education. That is what ordinary looks like when the leading killer of children is a firearm.

Other wealthy nations have cars, mental illness, despairing teenagers and violent entertainment. What they do not have is our gun policy. The difference is the gun, and the laws that decide who gets one.

## 3. The background-check gap

When the background check system is used, it works. The National Instant Criminal Background Check System has processed more than 500 million checks since 1998 and logged more than 2 million denials of sales to people legally barred from owning firearms (FBI).

The gap is where the system stops. Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed firearms dealer makes the sale. Private sellers, including many at gun shows and those arranging sales online, face no such requirement in most of the country. The result is a two-tier market: one in which a prohibited purchaser is screened out, and one in which the same purchaser can buy the same gun, no questions asked.

How big is the unchecked tier? In the best available national estimate, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017). That is roughly one acquisition in five. A felony record, a domestic violence conviction, a court's finding of dangerousness: none of it discovered, because nobody looked.

Americans broadly agree this should change. A national poll in June 2022 found 92% support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A policy with that kind of mandate is not waiting on public opinion. It is waiting on Congress.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 was a brutal year even by recent standards: 656 mass shootings, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023).

The massacres that define this era share a signature. At Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, 17 people were killed. At Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, 21 died, 19 of them children. In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, 18 were killed at a bowling alley and a bar. Each attack was carried out with a semiautomatic rifle and detachable high-capacity magazines, the configuration the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Congress enacted that ban in September 1994 as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, barring the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It let the law expire on Sept. 13, 2004. Federal evaluators found that criminal use of the banned weapons declined after the ban took effect (National Institute of Justice), and the market has since rebuilt itself around the banned design.

The usual rebuttal is that rifles of all types account for only a small share of gun murders, 297 of the 10,265 gun murders recorded in 2018, the FBI reports. But that is the wrong ledger for weapons built for volume rather than concealment. When an active shooter carries a semiautomatic rifle, the attack kills nearly twice as many people: an average of 4.25 deaths when such a rifle is present, against 2.49 when it is not (de Jager et al., JAMA, September 2018). And the decade the ban was in force stands apart from the years around it: mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period, 1994 to 2004 (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019).

## Recommendations

Congress should treat the leading killer of American children the way it treats every other leading cause of death: with urgency, funding and law. Four actions follow.

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check for every firearm sale and transfer, including private, gun show and online sales, with no exceptions, and appropriate the funds the FBI needs to process them.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 prohibition on assault weapons and on ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, covering manufacture and sale, and write the definition so the copycat designs engineered around the old feature list are covered too.
3. Fund gun violence prevention research. Establish a dedicated appropriations line for firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, building on the $25 million a year first appropriated in fiscal 2020 after a two-decade freeze, and scaled to the toll.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grants for states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws, with full due process protections, and fund training for the courts and law enforcement agencies expected to use them.

None of this is untested. Background checks already screen millions of sales a year and are backed by 92% of the country (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A federal assault weapons ban is not a thought experiment; it is a decade of American history, with data on both sides of it. The gaps are narrow, well documented and closable. The price of leaving them open was 46,728 lives in 2023.

Source detail for every figure in this brief appears in the Brief No. 9 data appendix.

# Safer Communities Brief No. 9: Data appendix

Supports: "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield. | Measure | Number |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths | 46,728 |
| Gun suicides | 27,300 (58% of total) |
| Gun homicides | 17,927 |
| Gun homicides, 2022 | 19,651 |
| Gun homicides, 2021 | 20,958 |

Notes: CDC WONDER final mortality data for 2023, as compiled by Johns Hopkins. The 2023 total is the third-highest annual number of gun deaths on record. Gun suicides reached a record high for the third consecutive year; suicides have been the majority of U.S. gun deaths every year since 1995. Homicides have declined from their 2021 peak. Per-day figures used in copy are derived: 46,728 divided by 365 equals about 128 deaths per day, or about one death every 11 minutes (JHU phrasing). Intent breakdowns appear here rather than in body copy, fact sheet or cards, per style sheet B2.

Source: Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic (CDC WONDER final data), June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf

## A2. Children and teens, 2023

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Gun deaths, children and teens | 2,566 |
| Death rate, children and teens | 3.7 per 100,000 |
| Leading cause of death | Firearms, fourth consecutive year |
| Deaths in named comparison causes | More than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancers |

Intent breakdown, 2023: homicide 63%; suicide 29%; unintentional 5%; undetermined or other 3%.

Notes: In this series, "children and teens" means ages 1-17, the JHU/CDC definition used for the ranking above (infants under 1 excluded). The age range is given here rather than in copy, per style sheet B3. For offices citing the broader band: the pooled rate for ages 1-19, 2021-2023, was 5.9 per 100,000.

## A3. The background-check estimate

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Owners who acquired a gun in the previous two years, no background check | 22% |
| NICS checks processed since 1998 | More than 500 million |
| NICS denials since 1998 | More than 2 million |
| Public support for checks on all gun buyers | 92% |

Notes: The 22% estimate comes from a 2015 national probability-based survey of 1,613 gun owners; the denominator is owners whose most recent acquisition fell within the previous two years, and the figure covers purchases, trades and other transfers. The series uses this estimate, not the older 1994 Cook and Ludwig figure of about 40%, because the 1994 figure counted gifts and inheritances and did not ask directly about background checks (per style sheet B4). NICS totals are FBI figures; the denial count covers federal denials processed by the FBI and excludes state point-of-contact denials. A denial means the check found a prohibiting record; it is not a prosecution.

Sources: Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017 (166(4):233-239), https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590 ; FBI, National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS), accessed October 2026, https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/more-fbi-services-and-information/nics ; Quinnipiac University, national poll release (background checks), June 8, 2022, https://poll.qu.edu/Poll-Release?releaseid=3848

| Measure | Number |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings | 656 |
| People killed | 712 |
| People injured | 2,692 |

Notes: GVA definition: an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter, in a single event at roughly the same time and location. GVA counted 647 mass shootings in 2022 and a record 689 in 2021, so 2023 was the second-highest year on record. Counts are as compiled in January 2024. Databases that define mass shootings by people killed rather than people shot, such as the AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass killing database, report far fewer incidents; the series uses GVA counts, per style sheet B5.

Source: Gun Violence Archive, Mass Shootings in 2023, data as compiled January 2024, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/reports/mass-shooting?year=2023 (also Axios, Mass shootings increased in 2023. But gun deaths went down, January 2024, https://www.axios.com/2024/01/09/mass-shooting-gun-violence-us-2023)

| Incident | Date | People killed | People wounded | Weapon |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Florida | Feb. 14, 2018 | 17 | 17 | Smith & Wesson M&P15 (AR-15-style rifle) |

| Measure | Number |
|---|---|
| Gun murders recorded, 2018 | 10,265 |
| Murders involving rifles, all types, 2018 | 297 |
| Murders involving rifles, 2017 | 390 |

## A7. Semiautomatic rifles and active shooter lethality

| Measure | Attacks with a semiautomatic rifle | Attacks without |
|---|---|---|
| Mean people killed | 4.25 | 2.49 |
| Mean people wounded | 5.48 | 3.02 |
| Mean killed or wounded | 9.72 | 5.47 |

Notes: Research letter comparing U.S. active shooter incidents with and without a semiautomatic rifle present. | Measure | Finding |
|---|---|
| Mass shooting fatalities during the ban period | 70% less likely to occur (relative rate 0.30, 95% CI 0.22-0.39) |
| Mass shooting-related deaths per 10,000 firearm homicides | 9 fewer during the ban period (p = 0.03) |
| Criminal use of the banned weapons | Declined after the ban took effect |

Notes: The federal assault weapons ban was enacted in the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, Public Law 103-322, on Sept. 13, 1994, and expired under its 10-year sunset on Sept. 13, 2004, 22 years before publication. The lethality findings are from an observational, pre-post analysis of open-source mass shooting data for 1981-2017, controlling for yearly trend; the ban period is compared with the years before and after. The National Institute of Justice evaluation found criminal use of the banned guns declined after the law took effect.

Sources: DiMaggio, Avraham, Berry, Bukur, Feldman, Klein, Shah, Tandon and Frangos, Changes in US Mass Shooting Deaths Associated With the 1994-2004 Federal Assault Weapons Ban: Analysis of Open-Source Data, Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019 (86(1):11-19), https://doi.org/10.1097/TA.0000000000002060 ; U.S. Congress, Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994, Public Law 103-322, September 1994, https://www.congress.gov/bill/103rd-congress/house-bill/3355 ; National Institute of Justice, Impacts of the 1994 Assault Weapons Ban: 1994-96, Research in Brief, 1997-1999, https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/173405.pdf

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers | 92% (7% opposed) |

- Assault weapons (house usage): the category defined in the outline, the firearms covered by the 1994 federal act: military-style semiautomatic firearms, including named models and semiautomatic rifles with detachable magazines and specified military features, together with ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds.

- Children and teens: ages 1-17 for the ranking and counts in A2; age range stated here per style sheet B3.

# New NPI brief to Congress: close the background-check gap, reinstate the assault weapons ban

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026 _ The Northgate Progress Institute on Tuesday releases Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

The brief's case rests on the numbers. Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, about one death every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens for the fourth consecutive year. Because federal law requires background checks only for sales by licensed dealers, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no check at all. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured.

"Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not fate. It is the price of two policy gaps Congress knows how to close," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield. "Universal background checks, a modern assault weapons ban, funded prevention research: none of it is exotic. What is missing is a vote."

The evidence section of the brief notes that mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the 1994-2004 period the federal assault weapons ban was in force. "We have already run this experiment," Whitfield said. "Congress should read the results."

The brief urges four actions: pass universal background checks on every sale and transfer; reinstate and update the lapsed 1994 assault weapons ban, including its limit on high-capacity magazines; fund gun violence prevention research at the CDC and the NIH; and create federal incentives for state extreme-risk laws.

Safer Communities Brief No. 9, its data appendix and a fact sheet for congressional offices will be available at [NPI website link].

The Northgate Progress Institute is a progressive policy think tank based in Washington, D.C.

DRAFT FOR EDITORIAL REVIEW: Not for release. NPI-PUB-2026-0457. Copy deadline: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Publication: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026.

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show: about one death every 11 minutes. Guns stayed the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, for the fourth consecutive year.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed dealer sells a gun. Among gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years, 22% did so without any background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017).
- The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and help states enact extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show. That is about one death every 11 minutes: roughly 128 people a day, every day, all year. Almost none of those deaths will make the national news. They happen in stairwells and garages and parked cars, to someone's parent, partner, child or friend.

No other high-income country lives with a toll like this. This one is not fixed in stone either. It is the product of policy, of gaps in American gun law wide enough to walk through. Two of the widest gaps are the subject of this brief: a background check system that covers only part of the gun market, and assault weapons that Congress once banned and let back on the shelves.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than this one: in 2023, for the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for America's children and teens, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer (CDC, 2023). Firearms killed 2,566 children and teens that year.

Each of those children had a classroom and a bedroom and a place at a lunch table. What they did not have was a country that treated gun deaths as a preventable problem. Parents send children to schools that run active-shooter drills. Grief counselors have become a fixture of American education. That is what ordinary looks like when the leading killer of children is a firearm.

Other wealthy nations have cars, mental illness, despairing teenagers and violent entertainment. What they do not have is our gun policy. The difference is the gun, and the laws that decide who gets one.

## 3. The background-check gap

When the background check system is used, it works. The National Instant Criminal Background Check System has processed more than 500 million checks since 1998 and logged more than 2 million denials of sales to people legally barred from owning firearms (FBI).

The gap is where the system stops. Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed firearms dealer makes the sale. Private sellers, including many at gun shows and those arranging sales online, face no such requirement in most of the country. The result is a two-tier market: one in which a prohibited purchaser is screened out, and one in which the same purchaser can buy the same gun, no questions asked.

How big is the unchecked tier? In the best available national estimate, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017). That is roughly one acquisition in five. A felony record, a domestic violence conviction, a court's finding of dangerousness: none of it discovered, because nobody looked.

Americans broadly agree this should change. A national poll in June 2022 found 92% support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A policy with that kind of mandate is not waiting on public opinion. It is waiting on Congress.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 was a brutal year even by recent standards: 656 mass shootings, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023).

The massacres that define this era share a signature. At Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, 17 people were killed. At Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, 21 died, 19 of them children. In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, 18 were killed at a bowling alley and a bar. Each attack was carried out with a semiautomatic rifle and detachable high-capacity magazines, the configuration the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Congress enacted that ban in September 1994 as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, barring the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It let the law expire on Sept. 13, 2004. Federal evaluators found that criminal use of the banned weapons declined after the ban took effect (National Institute of Justice), and the market has since rebuilt itself around the banned design.

The usual rebuttal is that rifles of all types account for only a small share of gun murders, 297 of the 10,265 gun murders recorded in 2018, the FBI reports. But that is the wrong ledger for weapons built for volume rather than concealment. When an active shooter carries a semiautomatic rifle, the attack kills nearly twice as many people: an average of 4.25 deaths when such a rifle is present, against 2.49 when it is not (de Jager et al., JAMA, September 2018). And the decade the ban was in force stands apart from the years around it: mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period, 1994 to 2004 (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019).

## Recommendations

Congress should treat the leading killer of American children the way it treats every other leading cause of death: with urgency, funding and law. Four actions follow.

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check for every firearm sale and transfer, including private, gun show and online sales, with no exceptions, and appropriate the funds the FBI needs to process them.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 prohibition on assault weapons and on ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, covering manufacture and sale, and write the definition so the copycat designs engineered around the old feature list are covered too.
3. Fund gun violence prevention research. Establish a dedicated appropriations line for firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, building on the $25 million a year first appropriated in fiscal 2020 after a two-decade freeze, and scaled to the toll.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grants for states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws, with full due process protections, and fund training for the courts and law enforcement agencies expected to use them.

None of this is untested. Background checks already screen millions of sales a year and are backed by 92% of the country (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A federal assault weapons ban is not a thought experiment; it is a decade of American history, with data on both sides of it. The gaps are narrow, well documented and closable. The price of leaving them open was 46,728 lives in 2023.

Source detail for every figure in this brief appears in the Brief No. 9 data appendix.

# NPI brief to Congress: close the background-check gap, reinstate the assault weapons ban

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026
The Northgate Progress Institute today releases Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

The case rests on the numbers: gun violence killed 46,728 people in 2023, about one death every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year. Because federal law requires checks only for licensed dealer sales, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no check. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, leaving 712 dead and 2,692 injured.

"Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not fate. It is the price of two policy gaps Congress knows how to close," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield. # Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | October 2026
By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show: about one death every 11 minutes. Guns stayed the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, for the fourth consecutive year.
- Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed dealer sells a gun. Among gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years, 22% did so without any background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017).
- The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, which left 712 people dead and 2,692 injured. Congress should pass universal background checks, reinstate and update the assault weapons ban that lapsed in 2004, fund gun violence research at the CDC and the NIH, and help states enact extreme-risk laws.

## 1. The toll

Gun violence killed 46,728 people in the United States in 2023, CDC final mortality data show. That is about one death every 11 minutes: roughly 128 people a day, every day, all year. Almost none of those deaths will make the national news. They happen in stairwells and garages and parked cars, to someone's parent, partner, child or friend.

No other high-income country lives with a toll like this. This one is not fixed in stone either. It is the product of policy, of gaps in American gun law wide enough to walk through. Two of the widest gaps are the subject of this brief: a background check system that covers only part of the gun market, and assault weapons that Congress once banned and let back on the shelves.

## 2. Children and teens

No statistic in this debate lands harder than this one: in 2023, for the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for America's children and teens, ahead of car crashes, drug overdoses and cancer (CDC, 2023). Firearms killed 2,566 children and teens that year.

Each of those children had a classroom and a bedroom and a place at a lunch table. What they did not have was a country that treated gun deaths as a preventable problem. Parents send children to schools that run active-shooter drills. Grief counselors have become a fixture of American education. That is what ordinary looks like when the leading killer of children is a firearm.

Other wealthy nations have cars, mental illness, despairing teenagers and violent entertainment. What they do not have is our gun policy. The difference is the gun, and the laws that decide who gets one.

## 3. The background-check gap

When the background check system is used, it works. The National Instant Criminal Background Check System has processed more than 500 million checks since 1998 and logged more than 2 million denials of sales to people legally barred from owning firearms (FBI).

The gap is where the system stops. Federal law requires a background check only when a licensed firearms dealer makes the sale. Private sellers, including many at gun shows and those arranging sales online, face no such requirement in most of the country. The result is a two-tier market: one in which a prohibited purchaser is screened out, and one in which the same purchaser can buy the same gun, no questions asked.

How big is the unchecked tier? In the best available national estimate, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check (Miller, Hepburn and Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, January 2017). That is roughly one acquisition in five. A felony record, a domestic violence conviction, a court's finding of dangerousness: none of it discovered, because nobody looked.

Americans broadly agree this should change. A national Quinnipiac University poll in June 2022 found 92% support for requiring background checks for all gun buyers. A policy with that kind of mandate is not waiting on public opinion. It is waiting on Congress.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings are the most visible form of American gun violence, and 2023 was a brutal year even by recent standards: 656 mass shootings, in which 712 people were killed and 2,692 injured (Gun Violence Archive, 2023).

The massacres that define this era share a signature. At Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland in 2018, 17 people were killed. At Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022, 21 died, 19 of them children. In Lewiston, Maine, in 2023, 18 were killed at a bowling alley and a bar. Each attack was carried out with a semiautomatic rifle and detachable high-capacity magazines, the configuration the federal assault weapons ban once restricted.

Congress enacted that ban in September 1994 as part of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act, barring the manufacture and civilian sale of assault weapons and of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. It let the law expire on Sept. 13, 2004. Federal evaluators found that criminal use of the banned weapons declined after the ban took effect (National Institute of Justice), and the market has since rebuilt itself around the banned design.

The usual rebuttal is that rifles of all types account for only a small share of gun murders, 297 of the 10,265 gun murders recorded in 2018, the FBI reports. But that is the wrong ledger for weapons built for volume rather than concealment. When an active shooter carries a semiautomatic rifle, the attack kills nearly twice as many people: an average of 4.25 deaths when such a rifle is present, against 2.49 when it is not (de Jager et al., JAMA, September 2018). And the decade the ban was in force stands apart from the years around it: mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period, 1994 to 2004 (DiMaggio et al., Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, January 2019).

## Recommendations

Congress should treat the leading killer of American children the way it treats every other leading cause of death: with urgency, funding and law. Four actions follow.

1. Pass universal background checks. Require a background check for every firearm sale and transfer, including private, gun show and online sales, with no exceptions, and appropriate the funds the FBI needs to process them.
2. Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban. Restore the 1994 prohibition on assault weapons and on ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, covering manufacture and sale, and write the definition so the copycat designs engineered around the old feature list are covered too.
3. Fund gun violence prevention research. Establish a dedicated appropriations line for firearm injury prevention research at the CDC and the NIH, building on the $25 million a year first appropriated in fiscal 2020 after a two-decade freeze, and scaled to the toll.
4. Incentivize state extreme-risk laws. Create grants for states that enact extreme-risk protection order laws, with full due process protections, and fund training for the courts and law enforcement agencies expected to use them.

None of this is untested. Background checks already screen millions of sales a year and are backed by 92% of the country (Quinnipiac University, June 2022). A federal assault weapons ban is not a thought experiment; it is a decade of American history, with data on both sides of it. The gaps are narrow, well documented and closable. The price of leaving them open was 46,728 lives in 2023.

Source detail for every figure in this brief appears in the Brief No. 9 data appendix.

Author: Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

# NPI brief to Congress: close the background-check gap, reinstate the assault weapons ban

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026
The Northgate Progress Institute today releases Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

The case rests on the numbers: gun violence killed 46,728 people in 2023, about one death every 11 minutes, and guns remained the leading cause of death for children and teens for the fourth consecutive year. Because federal law requires checks only for licensed dealer sales, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so with no check. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, leaving 712 dead and 2,692 injured.

"Forty-six thousand seven hundred twenty-eight deaths in a single year is not fate. It is the price of two policy gaps Congress knows how to close," said Dr. Jamal Whitfield. "Universal background checks, a modern assault weapons ban, funded prevention research: none of it is exotic. What is missing is a vote."

Mass shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the 1994-2004 period the federal ban was in force, the brief shows. "We have already run this experiment," Whitfield said. "Congress should read the results."

The brief urges Congress to pass universal background checks on every sale, reinstate and update the lapsed 1994 assault weapons ban including its limit on high-capacity magazines, fund gun violence prevention research at the CDC and NIH, and create incentives for state extreme-risk laws.
